title: Mock Interviews & Deliberate Practice
summary: Structuring practice so it actually transfers to the real thing — timed mocks, honest self-review, and progressing from untimed to cold, unfamiliar problems.

slides.markdown:
Solving a hundred problems untimed and alone at home doesn't reliably produce someone who performs well in a live, timed, watched round — the two activities exercise different muscles, and only one of them looks like the real interview. Volume of practice matters far less than whether the practice actually resembles the thing you're preparing for.

This topic covers why untimed solo practice doesn't transfer on its own, how to structure a full 45-minute mock end to end, giving and receiving useful feedback afterward, what to listen for reviewing a recording of yourself, tracking recurring failure patterns, and building a realistic multi-week plan before a real onsite.

slides.sectionTitle: Why untimed solo practice doesn't transfer
slides.markdown:
Solving a problem alone, untimed, with no one watching removes exactly the pressures that actually determine interview performance: a clock you can see, a person evaluating your narration in real time, and the social cost of going quiet or looking stuck. A candidate who can solve 200 problems this way can still freeze the first time someone is watching and a timer is visible, because that specific combination was never practiced.

This doesn't mean untimed practice is worthless — it's the right mode for *learning* a new pattern for the first time, when the goal is understanding, not performance. The mistake is treating volume in that mode as sufficient prep for the live, timed, watched version, and never practicing the version that actually resembles the real thing.

slides.sectionTitle: Structuring a 45-minute mock end to end
slides.markdown:
A realistic mock reproduces the actual round's shape, not just "solve a problem with a timer running." A workable structure: 2 minutes for the partner to present the prompt and for you to read it aloud, 3-5 minutes of clarifying questions, 1-2 minutes stating your approach and its complexity before coding, 20-25 minutes implementing while narrating out loud, 5-10 minutes testing and fixing bugs, and a few minutes at the end for the partner's questions or a follow-up twist.

The clarifying-questions and approach-stating phases are the ones candidates skip first when self-administering a mock, precisely because they feel like overhead when you're alone — which is exactly why a mock needs a partner or at least a strict script, not just a stopwatch on a real problem.

Useful feedback after a mock is specific and tied to a moment, not a general impression: "at minute 12 you jumped into coding before finishing your stated approach" is actionable; "you seemed a bit unclear" isn't. As the interviewer in someone else's mock, take real-time notes tied to timestamps or rough elapsed time rather than trying to reconstruct impressions afterward from memory.

As the candidate receiving feedback, resist the urge to explain away every point ("I was going to say that next") — the interviewer's read *is* the data, since a real interviewer would have formed the same impression without the benefit of your intended follow-up. Ask directly for the two or three things that would have moved the needle most, rather than a full transcript of every micro-observation.

slides.sectionTitle: Recording yourself: what to listen for
slides.markdown:
A recording surfaces things live feedback often misses because they're about *pacing and pattern*, not any single moment: how much dead silence there is between reading the prompt and saying anything, how often filler phrases ("um," "so basically," "like") crowd out actual content, and whether your stated complexity at the end actually matches the complexity of the code you wrote.

A specific, high-value habit: mute the recording and watch just your own pacing and body language for a minute, separate from listening to the content — it's much easier to notice you look frozen or are talking too fast when you're not also focused on following your own explanation. Reviewing a recording once a week, rather than after every single mock, keeps the habit sustainable without becoming its own chore.

slides.sectionTitle: Tracking the patterns in problems you keep failing
slides.markdown:
A single missed problem is just data; a log of missed problems over several weeks reveals whether there's a real pattern — always struggling with the same technique (say, interval problems), always running out of time on the second problem in a two-problem round, or always skipping clarifying questions when the prompt looks deceptively simple.

A minimal tracking log needs four fields per attempt: the problem's core pattern, whether you solved it within a reasonable time, what specifically went wrong if you didn't, and one note on what you'd do differently. Reviewing this log every week or two turns "I keep failing DP problems" from a vague feeling into a concrete, addressable gap — often the fix is targeted review of one specific sub-pattern, not "do more DP problems" in general.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: platform practice vs mock interviews vs pairing with a friend
slides.markdown:
| | Solo platform practice | Formal mock interview | Pairing with a friend |
|---|---|---|
| Best for | Learning a new pattern, building raw problem exposure | Full-fidelity rehearsal: pressure, narration, live feedback | Cheap, frequent narration practice without a strict script |
| What's missing | Pressure, narration, live feedback | Cost/scheduling if using a paid service | Consistency of a stranger's honest, unfiltered feedback |
| Cadence | Daily or near-daily | Weekly is realistic for most people | A few times a week |
| Failure mode if overused | Feels like progress without transferring to live performance | Too infrequent to build real narration habits on its own | Friends sometimes go easy on tough feedback |

A realistic plan uses all three for different purposes rather than treating any one as sufficient alone.

slides.sectionTitle: Progressing from untimed to cold problems
slides.markdown:
A useful practice progression has stages, and skipping straight to the hardest stage is what makes practice feel discouraging rather than productive: first, untimed practice on a known pattern to build the mechanism; then timed practice on a known pattern, to add pressure without also adding surprise; then timed practice on a *mixed*, unlabeled set of patterns, so pattern recognition itself gets exercised; finally, a fully cold problem under real interview conditions with no advance signal of which pattern it uses.

The last stage is the one candidates avoid longest because it's the most uncomfortable, and it's also the closest simulation of the real thing — a real interviewer doesn't announce "this is a sliding window problem" before starting the clock.

slides.sectionTitle: Building a multi-week practice plan before an onsite
slides.markdown:
A realistic plan works backward from the onsite date and allocates time across the progression in the previous slide rather than doing the same kind of practice every day until the date arrives. A rough shape for four to six weeks out: early weeks weighted toward untimed, pattern-by-pattern practice covering known gaps; middle weeks shift to timed, mixed-pattern sets; the final one to two weeks shift to mostly mock interviews and cold problems, tapering volume slightly right before the onsite rather than cramming hardest at the very end.

The common planning mistake is spending most of the available weeks in the easiest, most comfortable mode (untimed, known-pattern) and only reaching cold, timed mocks in the final days — which leaves too little repetition of the mode that actually resembles the real thing.

slides.sectionTitle: How many mocks is actually enough
slides.markdown:
There's no universal number, but a useful signal to watch is whether new mocks are still surfacing new failure patterns in your tracking log. If your last several mocks all reveal the same known issue rather than a new one, additional mocks in the exact same format have diminishing returns — the better use of time is deliberately practicing that specific known gap, then returning to full mocks to confirm it's fixed.

Overdoing formal mocks also has a real cost: they're the most expensive practice mode in time and often money, and burning all of them early leaves none left in the final week before the actual onsite, when a fresh, realistic rehearsal is most valuable.

The narration skill you're rehearsing in every mock is covered in depth in [thinking out loud](narrating-your-approach), and [pattern recognition](pattern-recognition) is the specific skill the cold, mixed-pattern practice stage is meant to build. For a much larger bank of practice problems organized by pattern, see `data-structures-algorithms`'s topic groups directly.
